text: No real quantum processor can directly execute every gate you've learned. Hardware implements a small, fixed set of native gates, and everything else gets rewritten in terms of them. This lesson explains why a small set is enough for everything, and verifies one concrete rewrite by hand.

Building a device that reliably implements even one precise, stable quantum operation is already hard engineering. Implementing dozens of different gates natively multiplies that difficulty many times over. So real processors implement a small handful of native gates well, and rely on the mathematical fact that this small set reaches everything else through composition — the same way a handful of classical logic gates, like NAND alone, builds any classical circuit.

The standard result is that the set H, T, and CNOT is universal: H and T together can be combined, in long enough sequences, to approximate any single-qubit rotation, while CNOT supplies all the entangling power a circuit needs. Here's a concrete, exact case, not just approximate: applying T twice squares its bottom-right entry, e to the i pi over 4, squared, which comes out to exactly i. That matches the S gate's matrix precisely — S equals T squared, with zero error term, verified by direct complex matrix multiplication.

When you write a circuit with convenient high-level gates, you're writing at a logical level. Before it runs, a compiler or transpiler rewrites every gate into the target hardware's specific native set — which is why the same logical circuit, run on two different real processors, can come back with very different real depth and gate count. And for continuous rotations in general, universal means arbitrarily close, not exact — S equals T squared is the rare case where the rewrite is perfectly exact.
Next lesson flips the direction: starting from a plain-English target state and working forward to a verified circuit that produces it — the actual day-to-day skill of writing quantum programs.
